summaries.example: Imagine three friends see that the teacher is late, but nobody says anything. Each friend knows the teacher is late, yet each may think they are the only one who knows. If one friend announces it aloud, everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so on. This shared understanding can help the friends decide what to do.
summaries.summary: Common knowledge is shared understanding that goes beyond everyone knowing a fact. It also includes everyone knowing that everyone knows it, and continuing through more and more levels. This matters because people often choose actions based on what they think others know and will do. A public announcement can make a fact common knowledge. The entry explains this idea through everyday puzzles and through games in which cooperation or success depends on careful reasoning about other people’s knowledge. It also notes that complete common knowledge may be difficult for real people to achieve, so weaker kinds of shared belief can sometimes be useful.
key_ideas: Knowing the same fact is not always enough. People may also need to know that others know it.
An open announcement can turn mutual knowledge into common knowledge.
Common knowledge helps people meet, cooperate, follow rules, and make plans.
Sometimes people fail to coordinate because they do not share enough information.
The source uses puzzles about messy faces, farmers, games, and a department store to show how reasoning about other people matters.
summaries.why_it_matters: Much of daily life depends on people making safe guesses about one another. We choose meeting places, follow traffic rules, cooperate on jobs, and make group plans partly because we expect others to understand the same situation. Learning about common knowledge helps explain both successful teamwork and surprising misunderstandings.

important_terms.definition: A fact that every person in a group knows, even if they do not know what the others know.
A fact that everyone knows, everyone knows that everyone knows, and this continues through many levels.
A way people act together successfully because they expect one another to act in certain ways.
A situation or action that people in a group can see or hear openly, so it can become shared knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: When does saying something aloud help a group work together?
Can a group know the same thing without having common knowledge?
Why might two people choose different meeting places even when both want to meet?
What could make an announcement fail to create common knowledge?

summaries.example: Consider a sequential game in which two players can stop early or continue, with later choices offering better joint outcomes but tempting each player to stop when their turn arrives. Backward induction reasons from the final possible move toward the beginning: if the last player would stop, the earlier player anticipates this, and so on. For this argument to predict play, each player must know not only the game and the other player’s rationality, but also what the other knows at the next decision point. The required higher-order knowledge becomes more demanding as the game grows longer.
summaries.summary: The entry analyzes common knowledge as a multi-agent epistemic concept: a proposition is common knowledge when every finite sequence of agents knows that the proposition holds. Mutual knowledge at one level is weaker, because it does not ensure that agents understand one another’s information. Formal models represent agents’ uncertainty with possible worlds and information partitions; common knowledge can then be identified with states reachable through chains of agents’ information cells. The concept explains why public announcements, conventions, equilibrium behavior, and backward induction can work. Yet its idealized infinite hierarchy raises questions about human reasoning and communication. The entry therefore also considers challenges to attainability and weaker notions such as common p-belief.
key_ideas: The central distinction is between everyone knowing A and everyone knowing that everyone knows A. The latter involves an indefinitely deep hierarchy.
Public events can generate common knowledge when agents perceive the event and understand that others can draw the same conclusion from it.
Common knowledge supports coordination, conventions, equilibrium reasoning, and some results about agreement in probability judgments.
Backward induction depends on assumptions about rationality, the game, and what each player knows about the next player’s knowledge.
The entry presents competing analyses, including hierarchical, partition-based, fixed-point, and socially richer accounts.
Skeptical arguments question whether human agents can attain full common knowledge; weaker belief concepts may better model some real situations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Common knowledge connects philosophy of knowledge with social coordination and game theory. It clarifies why shared information sometimes changes behavior, why a convention requires more than coincidental conformity, and why the justification of a predicted game outcome depends on assumptions about what players know about one another. It also warns that formal solution concepts can be sensitive to whether those assumptions are actually warranted.

important_terms.definition: A proposition is mutual knowledge at the first level when every agent knows it; this alone says nothing about what agents know about one another’s knowledge.
A proposition is common knowledge when it is mutual knowledge at every finite level: everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so on.
A formal representation of what an agent considers possible at a given state; it records the information the agent has without identifying the actual state completely.
Reasoning backward through a sequential game by eliminating choices that would not maximize the payoff of the player who moves later, then continuing toward the first move.
A game in which players move in sequence, observe earlier moves, and remember the history of play.
A stable pattern of choices in which no player benefits by changing their choice alone, given the others’ choices.
A recurring pattern of behavior that depends on mutual expectations and shared understanding, rather than merely on accidental agreement.
A weaker alternative to common knowledge in which agents assign a sufficiently high probability to a proposition and to increasingly many levels of others’ doing so.

questions_to_think_about: Why can an announcement add strategic value even when it states something everyone already knows?
How does a convention differ from two people coordinating by luck?
Should a player who reaches an unexpected decision point continue to apply backward induction?
What assumptions are needed before a disagreement in belief becomes philosophically puzzling?
Can common p-belief explain coordination that full common knowledge cannot?

summaries.example: Suppose four students have barbecue sauce on their faces, but each student can see only the others’ faces. At first, nobody knows whether they are messy. The cook announces that at least one person has sauce and rings a bell once for each round of thinking. If only one student were messy, that student would realize it after the first announcement. If two were messy, each would notice that the other did not clean up after the first ring and would realize they were messy after the second. In general, the messy students act after a number of rings matching the number of messy students. The announcement mattered because it made a fact shared at every level, not merely known separately by each?
summaries.summary: Common knowledge is a special kind of group understanding. Mutual knowledge means that each person knows a fact. Common knowledge goes further: each person knows it, knows that the others know it, knows that they know that the others know it, and so on. This structure matters because people often choose what to do by predicting other people’s choices and predictions. The entry illustrates the idea with the barbecue puzzle, the Farmers’ Dilemma, sequential games, and the department-store problem. It also discusses formal ways to represent knowledge, competing philosophical accounts, and weaker forms of shared belief when perfect common knowledge is unrealistic.
key_ideas: Mutual knowledge and common knowledge are different. Everyone may know a fact while being unsure whether others know it.
A public statement can create higher-order knowledge and change what people can logically infer.
Common knowledge helps explain cooperation, social conventions, and decisions in games.
In the Farmers’ Dilemma, both farmers would benefit from helping, but reasoning about future choices can lead them not to cooperate.
The department-store example shows a pure coordination problem: people want the same outcome but must select the same option.
Philosophers and social scientists disagree about how common knowledge should be analyzed and whether people can fully achieve it.
summaries.why_it_matters: Whenever people cooperate, they need some idea of what others understand and expect. Common knowledge helps explain why a spoken announcement, a familiar convention, or a shared meeting plan can coordinate behavior. It also explains why people can fail to cooperate even when they seem to possess the same basic information.

important_terms.definition: When each member of a group knows a fact, without necessarily knowing whether the others know it.
When everyone knows a fact, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and this pattern continues without a final level.
A group’s successful adjustment of actions when each person’s choice depends on what others are expected to do.
Information about which situations an agent thinks could be the actual one, given what the agent observes.
A repeated pattern of behavior that people follow because they expect others to follow it too.
A game in which players choose actions one after another and can observe the earlier choices.
A way of solving a sequential game by reasoning from the final choice back toward the first choice.
A belief shared through many levels, with agents assigning at least some chosen probability to the belief rather than claiming certainty.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the cook’s announcement help in the barbecue puzzle if everyone already sees at least one messy person?
When might a convention work even if nobody gives an explicit instruction?
Why can backward induction produce an outcome that is worse for both players?
What kinds of communication make shared knowledge stronger?
Is a very high level of mutual knowledge always a good substitute for common knowledge?
